questions.prompt: Holes in silicon have mobility \(\mu_p = 400\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\). What is their drift velocity in a field of \(E = 1\ \mathrm{kV/cm}\)?
questions.explanation:
\[v_{dr} = \mu_p E = 400 \times 1000 = 4\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm/s}\]
Holes drift ALONG the field (positive charge). Electrons drift against it, and at the same field they are faster: with \(\mu_n \approx 1000\) they would reach \(10^6\) cm/s.

questions.prompt: A field \(E\) points to the right in a silicon bar containing both electrons and holes (see figure). Which way do the electron drift current and the hole drift current point?
options: Both point to the right, along E, so they add
Electron current to the left, hole current to the right, so they partly cancel
Electron current to the right, hole current to the left
questions.explanation:
Holes move with \(E\): current to the right. Electrons move against \(E\) (to the left), but they carry negative charge, so their current is also to the right.
\[J_{drift} = q\,n\,\mu_n E + q\,p\,\mu_p E = q(n\mu_n + p\mu_p)E\]
Both terms have the sign of \(E\), so conductivities add. The carriers MOVE in opposite directions, but the CURRENTS don't.

questions.prompt: An n-type region has \(n = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) and \(\mu_n = 1000\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\). A field \(E = 10\ \mathrm{V/cm}\) is applied. What is the electron drift current density?
questions.explanation:
\[J_n = q\,n\,\mu_n E = (1.602\times10^{-19})(10^{16})(1000)(10) \approx 16.02\ \mathrm{A/cm^2}\]
The minority holes (\(10^4\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\)) contribute nothing measurable.

questions.prompt: A p-type silicon wafer is doped with \(N_A = 5\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), and \(\mu_p = 400\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\). What is its resistivity?
questions.explanation:
\(p_0 \approx N_A\), and the minority electrons are negligible:
\[\rho = \frac{1}{qN_A\mu_p} = \frac{1}{(1.602\times10^{-19})(5\times10^{15})(400)} \approx 3.12\ \Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm}\]
Common mistake: using the electron mobility. For a p-type sample the holes carry the current.

questions.prompt: An IC resistor is a bar of n-type silicon with \(N_D = 10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) (at this doping \(\mu_n = 700\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\)). It is \(L = 10\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) long, \(W = 2\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) wide and \(t = 0.5\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) thick. What is its resistance in kΩ?
questions.explanation:
\[\rho = \frac{1}{qN_D\mu_n} = \frac{1}{(1.602\times10^{-19})(10^{17})(700)} = 0.0892\ \Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm}\]
\[R = \rho\frac{L}{Wt} = 0.0892\times\frac{10\times10^{-4}}{(2\times10^{-4})(0.5\times10^{-4})} \approx 8917\ \Omega\]
That is about 8.92 kΩ. Convert µm to cm (\(1\ \mu\mathrm{m} = 10^{-4}\) cm) before mixing with Ω·cm.

questions.prompt: Reader Fig. 3.16 shows silicon mobility falling as the total dopant concentration rises (for electrons, from about 1400 down to about 100 cm²/(V·s)). Why?
options: Dopants add carriers, and carriers moving together slow each other down
The band gap closes at high doping, making carriers heavier
Dopants lower the thermal velocity of the carriers
Ionized dopant atoms break the lattice's periodicity and scatter carriers, so the mean free time τ (and μ = qτ/m*) drops
questions.explanation:
A perfect lattice doesn't scatter carriers. Lattice vibrations and impurities do (reader Sec. 3.2.7, 3.6.3). Each charged dopant ion is a scattering site, so more dopants mean shorter \(\tau\) and lower \(\mu\).
What matters is the TOTAL dopant density \(N_D + N_A\): compensating dopants still scatter, even though they cancel each other's carriers.
questions.figure_alt: Sketch of electron mobility falling as total dopant concentration increases from 10^14 to 10^19 per cm³.

questions.prompt: Compensated silicon: \(N_D = 10^{17}\) and \(N_A = 9\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). The electron mobility depends on the TOTAL dopant density: \(\mu_n \approx 600\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\) at \(1.9\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), but \(\approx 1250\) at \(10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). What is the resistivity?
questions.explanation:
Carriers: \(n_0 = N_D - N_A = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). Scattering: all \(1.9\times10^{17}\) ions scatter, so \(\mu_n \approx 600\).
\[\rho = \frac{1}{q\,n_0\,\mu_n} = \frac{1}{(1.602\times10^{-19})(10^{16})(600)} \approx 1.04\ \Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm}\]
Gotcha: using the mobility for \(10^{16}\) (1250) gives 0.50 Ω·cm, a factor of 2 too low. Using \(n = 10^{17}\) gives about 0.10 Ω·cm. Net doping sets the carrier count; total doping sets the mobility.

questions.prompt: In intrinsic silicon under a field, electrons drift one way and holes the other. A student says: 'equal numbers of carriers moving in opposite directions, so the currents cancel.' What is right?
options: The currents cancel exactly, so intrinsic silicon carries no drift current
Only the faster electrons carry current
questions.explanation:
Opposite motion of opposite charges gives current in the SAME direction. The conductivity is \(\sigma = q(n\mu_n + p\mu_p)\), a sum of positive terms.
Gotcha: the subtraction \(\mu_n - \mu_p\) would be right for the net PARTICLE flux, not the current. (Reader Eq. 3.14 writes \(J = J^+ - J^-\) with \(J^-\) carrying its own negative sign, which can mislead; the conductivity in Eq. 3.15 is a sum.)

questions.prompt: In p-type silicon with \(N_A = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) (\(\mu_n = 1000\), \(\mu_p = 400\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\), \(n_i = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\)), what is the ratio of electron drift current to hole drift current, \(J_n/J_p\), in a uniform field? Scientific notation is fine.
questions.explanation:
\(p_0 = 10^{16}\), \(n_0 = n_i^2/N_A = 10^{4}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). Both see the same \(E\):
\[\frac{J_n}{J_p} = \frac{n_0\mu_n}{p_0\mu_p} = \frac{10^{4}\times1000}{10^{16}\times400} = 2.5\times10^{-12}\]
Gotcha: the higher electron mobility doesn't come close to making up for \(10^{12}\) times fewer electrons. Minority carriers essentially never carry DRIFT current. When minority carriers do matter (in diodes), they move by diffusion.

questions.prompt: Preview of the MOSFET channel: a later skill models a transistor channel as a thin sheet of electrons. Suppose the sheet holds \(10^{12}\) electrons per cm² with \(\mu_n = 500\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\). It is \(W = 10\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) wide and \(L = 1\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) long, with 0.1 V across its length. Treating it as drift of a sheet (current = width × sheet charge × velocity), what current flows, in µA?
questions.explanation:
Field along the channel: \(E = V/L = 0.1/(10^{-4}\ \mathrm{cm}) = 10^{3}\ \mathrm{V/cm}\), so \(v = \mu_n E = 5\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm/s}\).
Sheet charge: \(Q = qN_s = 1.602\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{C/cm^2}\).
\[I = W\,Q\,v = (10^{-3}\ \mathrm{cm})(1.602\times10^{-7})(5\times10^{5}) \approx 80.1\ \mu\mathrm{A}\]
In the MOSFET skills the gate voltage sets \(Q\), and this same drift picture becomes the triode-region current. More sheet charge or a wider device gives proportionally more current.

questions.prompt: Preview of total current: two bars, A (\(\sigma_A = 2\ \mathrm{S/cm}\)) and B (\(\sigma_B = 0.5\ \mathrm{S/cm}\)), with the same cross-section are joined end to end and carry a steady current. How do the fields inside them compare?
options: \(E_A = E_B\), since the bars are in series
\(E_B = 4E_A\): the same current density needs a larger field in the less conductive bar
questions.explanation:
In steady state no charge piles up, so the current density is the same in both bars: \(J = \sigma_AE_A = \sigma_BE_B\). That gives \(E_B/E_A = \sigma_A/\sigma_B = 4\).
This is the same as series resistors: the bigger resistance takes the bigger share of the voltage. The total-current skill uses this boundary condition (reader Eq. 3.58–3.60).

questions.prompt: Preview of temperature effects in transistors: in a doped resistor, the carrier count is set by the dopants and barely changes with temperature, while lattice scattering makes the mobility fall roughly as \(\mu \propto T^{-3/2}\). By what factor does the resistance of an n-type silicon resistor rise from 300 K to 400 K?
questions.explanation:
\(R \propto \rho = 1/(qN_D\mu)\), with \(N_D\) fixed, so \(R \propto 1/\mu \propto T^{3/2}\):
\[\frac{R(400)}{R(300)} = \left(\frac{400}{300}\right)^{3/2} \approx 1.54\]
Unlike pure silicon, whose resistance collapses as \(n_i\) grows, a doped resistor behaves like a metal. The same mobility drop is why a hot MOSFET carries LESS current at a fixed gate voltage, which makes power transistors share current well.
